In Boston visit relatives often. Never heard the city called The Hub. Ever.
A memorable debut but I Must adMit that I wish the answers were as rigorously themed as the clues
Mamma Mia, I found the clues to be mildly maddening. But I must say it was masterfully made.
Not worthy of a Wednesday. The M clues seemed contrived. But others may love it. ATEN had me puzzled for a minute.

I was not a fan of today's puzzle.  All the hyphenated Ms kind of gave me a headache and made it hard to focus on the clues I as trying to read.

Also the main spanner of the puzzle was a very specific piece of Harry Potter trivia MISCHIEF MANAGED.  Such an odd phrase you can't even really piece it together without almost all crossers, and half the crossers were weak.  Weird acronyms like EDF, ICI.

Then who the heck has heard of BATH, Maine?  Fewer people than Natick, Mass.

Getting a headache just looking at the clues combined with the major spanner being a giant Natick requiring extremely specific information that even big fans of the series might not remember.  Frustrating puzzle.
I didn’t pay attention to the constructor’s name until completing the puzzle. That gave me quite a smile. Congratulations on a marvelous, mirthful, mischievous debut, Mr. Motz. Very enjoyable.

Mmmmmmm. I liked the theme answers, but thought the cluing was too constricted by the  MANDM gimmick.  Clues like marmot or marmoset for ANIMAL and Mild-mannered characteristic for HYPHEN are among my least favorite.

There was a little 50s / 60s theme going on.  As a baseball fan since childhood, I was fortunate enough to have seen MICKEYMANTLE play, in the early 60s, and happy to see him pop up in the puzzle.  I was also happy to see the smoothest soul singer, SAM Cooke also crop up. I love his pop hits like Cupid, and Wonderful World, but A Change Is Gonna Come gives me the shivers every time I hear it.
Couldn't decide whether I loved it or hated it (the bolded Ms made my head hurt!). But I did get a chuckle when I noticed the constructor's name.

Well that was annoying.  Different, certainly, but just annoying.  It would have been okay if it were more interesting or more clever, bit it was not.  Overall puzzle play was fine but the excessive bolding came off as grade school level and there was no payoff.

I quite liked the clue for Hyphen, which more than made up for the green paintery of "A Ten" (sigh).

We've had worse.  :)
All the bolded m’s were annoying. The editors should have left off the bolding and let the theme dawn on us, instead of hammering it at us.

MISCHIEF MANAGED! Minimally mindbending/mysterious? Maybe. Massively merry, mirthful moments? Mm-hmm!

May many more manifest, Mac! Masterful!

I loved it! Partly because of the rigorous discipline required to make EVERY SINGLE CLUE work.  Whenever I see that, I have to tip my hat.

But the clincher for me, which admittedly would not do much for the vast majority of solvers, is that I grew up in Moline, Illinois.  Great to see the old home town get a shout out, particularly since my primary mementos of it are shirts with the letter "M" on them!  

It's like when were are watching Jeopardy, and the correct response is either "What is 'Hamlet'?" or "What is 'Raleigh'?"  Our two dogs, Hamlet and Raleigh, always watch Jeopardy with us.

Take your pleasures where you find them  If they are a little goofy, so much the better.

Clue 3 Down is "Maximum degree i math" for NTH.

It is true that, informally, "nth" is used to mean a maximum extent.

But nobody uses "nth" in math to mean a maximum degree.

It sure would be nice if the editors bothered to fact-check the crossword clues.
Congrats and thanks for a fun debut!

For those unhappy with MISCHIEFMANAGED (apart from those who just don’t want Harry Potter or JK Rowling in a puzzle, which I’m not getting into)—it’s not a Natick. It’s two common words making a fun phrase. You already know they start with M. If you don’t know it you can figure it out with some crosses and isn’t that the fun part of a puzzle? I did know it, but wish I didn’t, because I would have enjoyed puzzling it out, and if it were a similar phrase from  popular culture that I hadn’t heard that would have been perfectly ok with me. I keep coming back to this, folks. Is your goal of solving crosswords really only to enter things you’ve already heard of?

I was almost halfway through the puzzle before I noticed all the M’s in the clues. Then the whole theme came together (nothing passes me by) 😂. Many congratulations on making a most magnificent puzzle Mr. Mac Motz ! I enjoyed it immensely.
I don't get this puzzle at all. The theme gives itself away right at the top and there's nothing to really figure out. The whole thing was cutesy rather than challenging or inventive.
More fun puzzles like these, please.

Understanding the need for two m's I still found [Munificent man]--SHARER to be a letdown since I was looking for someone thus gendered as the answer, like MENSCH. Or is that Making a Mountain out of a Molehill? There were a couple other clues, as My Main Man Marshall pointed out, where the M's constricted the quality of clue/fill. But it must have been fun clueing this, and it surely deserves its publication in the Times. 

Not knowing EFT as financial e-transfer of funds (I see EFT as somewhere between newt and salamander), I couldn't decide what shouldn't be missed with CU_. A golfer in a tournament can miss the CUT, so I put TFT. But I also, when expectorating or playing beer pong, two of my favorite passtimes, often miss the CUP, so I considered PFT an alternative. If I was a ruminant I'd possibly miss my CUD... All that to say that I missed my CUE on that one.

Funny, recurring answers a few days apart, WEN appearing Aug. 28 with about the same clue. MATRON: Housemother on Aug. 26, a word that doesn't often appear here, and the variety of cluing over the years speaks to its elusive meaning: dignified woman, supervisor of a female dorm (or prison), ladies' club member; pre-Shortz: dowager, ladies' room attendant, Grande Dame, married woman (1961), mature married woman (1992).

Never let it be said I was too proud to say that an early week puzzle gave me fits, because this one did.

If I had to analyze, I'd say that the emphasis on the "M"s was priming my brain with an M, so I wanted to start the answers with an "M" as well.

Well, that *M*ethod leads to *m*adness.

While fighting that off, 38A (the one with the "Harry Potter" clue, Andrzej) was a Massive Mystery to me.  Crosses got me to something + MANAGED.  I didn't know 27D with the Marseille Map, but I was banking on "ile".  Mistake there too.

For 35D, I couldn't decide between "ebt", "edt", and a couple of other less likely things.

And I wasn't sure about the stinky fruit, either.

So I fought and fought and fought with vowels in a couple of places, all the while fending off those *m*assive *m* attacks.

It was only when I realized that the Harry Potter thing was awfully close to MISCHIEFMANAGED, that I finally found the combination.

But it felt very brute force, which, if I'm honest, isn't a bad feeling for a squirrelly little snowflake like myself.

I simply *did not see* the bold letters in the clues on my Samsung phone, and never noticed the repeated 'M's in the answers. *M*aking the entire theme *m*oot. 

And other than the 'mid' theme? Maybe meh?

FWIW, there are some residences in New York City that are *not* apartment buildings. New York City has five boroughs (also called counties). They all have homes with porches, although some more than others.

“Maxims discouraging misconduct” are MORES.  MORAYS are eels.  Homophones, different spellings.  A rare editorial and setter mistake.  It's annoying because clueing "MORAYS" would have been simple:  "Marine Menaces" for example.

So, if I may be the anti-Lewis for a moment:

The chief trick of this puzzle, for me, was psychological: trying *not* to make all the entries begin with "M." That held me up for a while, especially at first.

Also, for those of us who solve from Alaska to Florida, having the revealer at 1A made the experience a bit of a let-down. Of course, some of the entries, including the one 15-letter spanner, did have double-M alliteration, but nothing in the works to mark that they were "special."  Also, the "metric units" (1D) entry might have worked as an additional revealer, but that didn't seem to be the intent.

Usually, I'm a fan of puzzles with tight construction restraints--lipograms and the like. But this one didn't work. Moving the revealer to Florida, and eliminating all the alliterative clues, would have made this a perfectly enjoyable, Monday puzzle.

You may like or not like this puzzle, but for anyone who thinks it was easy to come up with these clues, I offer a challenge:

Take yesterday's puzzle and try creating clues that meet the constraint Mac put on himself.  I'll bet you won't get very far.

Mmmmmm…I found it tasty!

Don’t forget that if your mileage varies on any given puzzle, that’s not a fault of the creator or the editors.  It’s _your_ mileage that varied.

Remember to be kind, y’all.  Take care.
